headline: Roku's First OLED TVs Start at $699 With Up to $400 Off
summary: Roku's new 55-inch and 65-inch Pro Series OLED TVs are now available at significantly reduced prices, making them the most affordable modern OLED options.
details: Roku has launched its first-ever OLED TVs, with the 55-inch Pro Series model initially priced at $999. This TV boasts a 120Hz refresh rate OLED panel, four HDMI 2.1 ports, and support for Dolby Vision and HDR 10 Plus.

Currently, Amazon is offering a substantial discount on the 55-inch model. By using the code ROKUOLED300 at checkout, customers can save $300, bringing the price down to $699, making it the most affordable modern 55-inch OLED TV available.
For those interested in a larger screen, the 65-inch Pro Series model is also on sale. With the code ROKUOLED400, shoppers can get $400 off the regular $1,299 price, reducing it to $799.

While these models haven't been tested yet, they appear to be a strong choice for those seeking great picture quality without a premium price tag. The TVs come with Roku's built-in software, eliminating the need for an external streaming device.

The Pro Series includes a backlit Roku remote and supports features like auto low latency mode and AMD FreeSync Premium for an enhanced gaming experience. A more advanced Pro Series LX is set to release in October, promising double the brightness and a 144Hz refresh rate.

topic: us appeals court upholds pentagon designation of anthropic as supply chain risk
headline_marked: Appeals court [[lets Pentagon designate Anthropic]] a supply-chain risk
headline: Appeals court lets Pentagon designate Anthropic a supply-chain risk
summary: A federal appeals court refused to overturn the US Department of Defense's designation of Anthropic as a supply-chain risk, allowing the ban on Claude AI models to continue.
details: An appeals court has upheld the Pentagon's designation of Anthropic, the AI company behind Claude, as a supply-chain risk. This decision means the US government can continue to block Anthropic's AI models from its systems.

The court found that the Department of Defense had sufficient grounds to label Anthropic a risk, citing the company's restrictions on Claude's capabilities. Anthropic stated it is considering further legal options, including appeals to higher courts.

Previously, the Pentagon sanctioned Anthropic under specific laws, aiming to remove Claude from federal government use. Anthropic executives had stated they would not permit their AI to support autonomous weapons or domestic surveillance, a stance deemed a national security risk by Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth.

While a federal judge in San Francisco previously dismissed one of the supply-chain risk labels, Friday's ruling by the DC Circuit Court of Appeals allows the other designation to remain indefinitely. This legal battle could continue for years.
The designations have reportedly impacted Anthropic's revenue by causing customer concerns, though the company has also touted recent sales growth and is preparing for a potential IPO.

The Pentagon has not detailed its progress in finding alternatives to Claude, with reports suggesting the use of models like SpaceX's Grok, Google's Gemini, and OpenAI's GPT. Some employees at Google and OpenAI have raised ethical objections to their companies partnering with the US military.
